quote: vielleicht giebt es aber besondere Flächen bei denen dies dennoch möglich ist.
english: but perhaps there are special surfaces for which this is nevertheless possible.
topic: Three short notes: Minkowski's conjecture that a closed surface of flexible but inextensible material cannot be continuously bent (especially the sphere); whether all ruler-and-compass constructions can be done with compass alone; and a task to prove that no number in the cyclotomic field other than the root of unity has discriminant equal to the field discriminant.

triage.modern_statement: Is there a closed (compact, boundaryless) surface in R^3 that can be flexed? That means a continuous, non-trivial family of isometric deformations: the surface bends without stretching, and the motion is not just a rigid motion of space. The note is the counterpart to Minkowski's conjecture that closed surfaces, and the sphere in particular, are rigid. The answer depends on the smoothness class: (a) smooth or analytic closed surfaces; (b) closed polyhedral surfaces with rigid faces hinged along the edges.
triage.answered_by: Minkowski's conjecture was confirmed for the sphere by H. Liebmann in 1899 ('Eine neue Eigenschaft der Kugel', Göttinger Nachrichten). S. Cohn-Vossen extended it to all ovaloids (closed convex surfaces) in 1927. Hilbert's 'special surfaces' turned out to exist in the polyhedral case: R. Connelly gave the first flexible closed embedded polyhedron in 1977 (Publ. Math. IHES 47), and K. Steffen later found a 9-vertex example. Whether a smooth, closed, non-convex surface can flex is still a long-standing open problem.

evidence.claim: Liebmann (1899) showed the sphere is not bendable. Cohn-Vossen's 1927 paper proved that ovaloids admit no bending, and Darboux showed small analytic surface pieces are bendable.
Bibliographic record: Liebmann, 'Eine neue Eigenschaft der Kugel', Nachr. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen 1899, pp. 44-55.
Every smooth closed convex surface in R^3 is rigid. Whether a flexible smooth, closed, non-convex surface exists is a long-open problem.
Connelly found the first counterexample to the Rigidity Conjecture for closed non-self-intersecting polyhedra in 1977, and Steffen soon found a 9-vertex flexible polyhedron.
Reference: R. Connelly, 'A counterexample to the rigidity conjecture for polyhedra', Publ. Math. IHES 47 (1977) 333-338.
Cohn-Vossen also gave a surface of revolution that is infinitesimally flexible (the 'flying saucer'). Liebmann proved strictly convex ovaloids are infinitesimally rigid.
Work on flexible closed polyhedral surfaces and on the smooth case is still going on (2025 'base + crinkle' construction; 2025 twinning construction of flexible polyhedra).
Recent seminar work on flexible smooth immersions of cylinders in R^3 treats isometric flexibility of smooth surfaces as a classical question still under study.

triage.why: Hilbert's note asks whether some closed surfaces, unlike the sphere, might be bendable after all. This is the classical problem of rigidity versus flexibility of closed surfaces. Minkowski's part was proved: Liebmann showed the sphere is rigid in 1899, and Cohn-Vossen extended this to all convex closed surfaces in 1927. Hilbert's suspicion that special flexible surfaces exist was confirmed for polyhedra by Connelly in 1977. For smooth closed surfaces it is still open, and current papers describe it as a long-open problem. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. I can't tell from the note whether Hilbert meant smooth surfaces or would also count polyhedra, so the verdict is 'open_and_known' for the smooth case, with the polyhedral case solved. That ambiguity is why confidence is medium.
